fetched_contents.text: Microwave-induced heavy metal removal from dewatered biosolids for cost-effective composting Introduction Biosolids are the final products of sludge produced during sewage treatment in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) (Margui et al., 2016). With the continuing rapid growth of human populations and the global trend towards urbanization, an increasingly large amount of sewage and its resulting biosolids are being produced worldwide (Mateo-Sagasta et al., 2015). For example, the WWTPs in China yielded more than 6 million metric tons of dry biosolids in 2013, with a mean annual growth of 13% from 2007 to 2013 (Yang et al., 2015). It has been a serious challenge for many countries to properly dispose the increasing amount of biosolids (Londono et al., 2017), especially considering that conventional disposal methods, such as sanitary landfilling and incineration, are neither environmentally friendly nor sustainable (Abusoglu et al., 2017). An alternative to unsustainable disposal practices is the post-composting of biosolids for potential use as organic fertilizers in agricultural soils, as they are usually rich in diverse plant nutrients (e.g., N and P) and organic matter (Sharma et al., 2017). With the land application of biosolids, the physical, chemical, and biological properties of the amended soils (e.g., porosity, moisture, pH, cation exchange capacity, humus content, microbial biomass, and enzymatic activities) can be greatly improved (Koutroubas et al., 2014; Lloret et al., 2016). As a result, agricultural production can be enhanced with minimal need for energy-intensive synthetic fertilizers, while the nutrient losses via leaching and surface runoff can be effectively mitigated (Alcantara et al., 2015; Arduini et al., 2018). Due to its waste-to-resource nature, land application of biosolids has earned popularity in recent years (Sharma et al., 2017). For instance, at least 55% of the biosolids (i.e., 17.8 million metric tons of dry biosolids) generated in the United States are utilized to regain soil fertility and improve soil properties in agricultural lands and forests (Miller-Robbie et al., 2015). However, the commercialization of biosolid-derived fertilizers for agriculture must be performed cautiously, as it is widely known that biosolids often contain toxic metal residues (i.e., heavy metals) (Ashekuzzaman et al., 2019). The species and concentrations of heavy metals in biosolids produced in different WWTPs may differ due to dissimilar chemical compositions of wastewater and different treatment technologies (Westerhoff et al., 2015). Commonly found heavy metals in biosolids include, but are not limited to As, Cd, Cu, Pb, Hg, Mo, Ni, Se, and Zn (Lara-Villa et al., 2011; Muchuweti et al., 2005). Heavy metals in sewage can be from the merging of industrial wastewater, commercial products, and storm water runoff, among other sources (Westerhoff et al., 2015). Besides their uptake by plants, the increased leaching of heavy metal ions into groundwater has also been observed in field studies (Koutroubas et al., 2014; Latare et al., 2014). Depending on the levels of toxicity and dosages of the heavy metals, as well as the land application rate, untreated or inappropriately treated biosolids may be detrimental to plant growth and harm the food web (Koupaie and Eskicioglu, 2015). The presence of toxic heavy metals in biosolids is the major obstacle to their land application (Margui et al., 2016). It is necessary to extract heavy metals from biosolids and lower their contents below the regulation limits prior to any agricultural usage (Sharma et al., 2017). Most heavy metals can be extracted chemically, physically, and/or biologically (Camargo et al., 2016). Physical methods, such as heat treatment (Shi et al., 2013) and electroremediation (Elicker et al., 2014), are plagued by high costs. Chemical methods employ a variety of metal extractants, including inorganic acids (Gheju et al., 2011), organic acids (Dacera and Babel, 2006), salts (Navarro-Gonzalez et al., 2017), chelating agents (Manouchehri et al., 2006), and mixed reagents (Du et al., 2015). Although the costs of chemical methods are lower than those of physical methods, the risk of secondary pollution due to chemical residues is discouraging (Camargo et al., 2016). Biological methods, such as bioleaching (Wen et al., 2013) and vermicomposting (Azizi et al., 2013), are economically viable and environmentally friendly, but they are demanding in terms of the requisite environmental conditions and may not be suitable for certain high-toxicity metals (Camargo et al., 2016). Although biological methods have gained almost equal prominence in recent years, chemical methods are still the most commonly used and widely studied because of their efficiency and simplicity (Camargo et al., 2016). In an early study, the performance of heavy metal extraction was explored using two inorganic acids (nitric and hydrochloric), two organic acids (citric and oxalic), and one strong chelator (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, i.e., EDTA) (Gheju et al., 2011). It was found that organic reagents had the highest removal efficiencies, followed by EDTA. However, none of the extractants alone was able to effectively remove all species of heavy metals. Hence, the combined use of two or more reagents was suggested to enhance removal efficiencies (Gheju et al., 2011). In a later study, nitrite was added during sludge acidification to enhance metal removal (Du et al., 2015), and a significant improvement in Cu removal from 3–7% to 45–64% and in Zn removal from ∼70% to >81% was observed; this was attributed to the disruption of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) assisted by free nitrous acid (Du et al., 2015). Microwave treatment improves wastewater treatment efficiency by reducing metal load, accelerating recovery, and enabling better sludge reuse or secondary treatment. The evidence suggests that heavy metals in biosolids can be toxic and must be lowered below regulatory limits before agricultural use or reuse, and that conventional methods are costly or environmentally risky [N1-F1]. Microwave-induced extraction and stabilization studies indicate that microwave processing can remove or immobilize heavy metals from sludge, which directly lowers downstream treatment burden by reducing the concentration of metals in the remaining sludge [N1-F1][N1-R1][N6-R1]. 

Reduced metal load lowers downstream burden because biosolids with lower heavy-metal content are easier and safer to handle, and less likely to contaminate subsequent treatment steps or land application [N1-F1]. In the microwave-stabilized biosolids study, copper ions were stabilized after microwave treatment, implying that metals are no longer freely available in the sludge matrix and thus less likely to interfere with downstream processes [N1-R1]. The same study also notes that microwave pretreatment can improve dewatering and pathogen inactivation, which may reduce the volume and complexity of downstream sludge handling [N2-R2].

Faster or more complete recovery shortens treatment time because microwave-assisted leaching has been shown to be more efficient than conventional heating. The 1996 EPA comparison study found that microwave heating improved precision and effectiveness compared to conventional hot plate heating for leaching key elements such as cadmium, chromium, copper, lead, nickel, and zinc [N4-F2]. This implies that microwave treatment can achieve similar or better extraction efficiency in less time, which is especially valuable in wastewater treatment where rapid turnaround is important [N4-F2]. The biosolids study also reports that microwave treatment can induce immobilization with relatively low exposure time and power, suggesting that the method can be time-effective while still achieving significant metal removal [N1-F1][N1-R3].

Sludge reuse or secondary treatment benefits improve overall system performance by making biosolids more suitable for land application, composting, or resource recovery. The biosolids study emphasizes that biosolids are often rich in nutrients and organic matter, and that their land application can improve soil properties and reduce reliance on synthetic fertilizers [N1-F1]. However, heavy metals in biosolids limit their use because they can leach into groundwater and harm plants and food webs [N1-F1]. Microwave-induced removal or stabilization makes biosolids safer for reuse, which enhances the value of wastewater treatment as a waste-to-resource system [N1-F1][N6-R1]. The comparison with conventional methods also suggests that microwave treatment is cheaper than some physical methods and may be more compatible with secondary treatment goals than more expensive or complex alternatives [N4-R5].

Taken together, microwave treatment enhances wastewater treatment efficiency by reducing the metal load that downstream processes must handle, speeding up recovery through more effective leaching or immobilization, and enabling safer, more valuable sludge reuse or secondary treatment [N1-F1][N4-F2][N6-R1].

Microwave treatment improves heavy metal extraction from wastewater sludge by triggering physical and chemical changes that make metals more available for recovery. The most direct evidence comes from microwave-induced heavy metal removal from dewatered biosolids, which describes a novel microwave-mediated method for extracting heavy metals from sludge [N1-F1][N2-R1]. The same study notes that microwave pretreatment can improve dewatering and pathogen inactivation, suggesting that it alters sludge structure in ways that favor metal release [N2-R2]. A separate microwave-assisted leaching study found that microwave heating improved precision and effectiveness compared to conventional heating for leaching metals such as cadmium, chromium, copper, lead, nickel, and zinc, showing that microwave heating can enhance extraction efficiency [N4-F2].

The physical and chemical changes triggered by microwaves include heating, desorption, and structural disruption. The biosolids study states that microwave treatment can induce immobilization of heavy metals, which implies that microwaves can both release metals from the sludge matrix and then stabilize them under controlled conditions [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The 1996 EPA comparison study explains that microwave heating improves precision and effectiveness by better controlling the reaction environment, which likely contributes to more efficient desorption and leaching [N4-F2]. The evidence also supports the idea that microwave pretreatment can change sludge structure: in biosolids, microwave treatment improves dewatering and inactivates pathogens, indicating that it modifies the physical arrangement and organic matrix of sludge to make metals more accessible [N2-R2].

Heating, desorption, and chelation interact during extraction. The biosolids study notes that most heavy metals can be extracted chemically using reagents such as inorganic acids, organic acids, salts, chelating agents, and mixed reagents [N1-F1]. In the context of microwave treatment, the study explicitly says that organic reagents had the highest removal efficiencies, followed by EDTA, and that combined reagents were needed to effectively remove all metal species [N1-F1]. This suggests that microwave heating creates favorable conditions for chelation and desorption. The same study also mentions that nitrite was added during sludge acidification to enhance metal removal, with free nitrous acid disrupting extracellular polymeric substances and improving removal of Cu and Zn [N1-F1]. This indicates that microwave treatment may not only heat the sludge but also create a chemical environment in which chelating agents and other reagents can act more effectively [N1-F1].

Which metal species are most effectively recovered and why depends on the extractant and the sludge matrix. The biosolids study reports that organic reagents had the highest removal efficiencies, followed by EDTA, while combined reagents were needed to recover all species [N1-F1]. This implies that metals with stronger coordination to organic ligands or sludge-bound complexes are more readily removed by chelation. The study also notes that EDTA washing and hydraulic cavitation were used to remove toxic metals from sewage sludge, and that EDTA and process water were recycled in a closed-loop process [N2-R5]. This supports the idea that chelating agents are particularly useful for metals such as Cu, Zn, Cd, Pb, and possibly other transition metals that form stable complexes with EDTA [N2-R2][N2-R5]. The microwave-assisted leaching study suggests that copper, chromium, nickel, lead, cadmium, and zinc are the primary metals of interest, and that microwave heating can improve extraction efficiency for these species [N4-F2].

Microwave pretreatment can change sludge structure to favor extraction by altering the physical and chemical environment of the sludge. The biosolids study says microwave pretreatment improves dewatering and inactivates pathogens, which implies that it can break down organic matter and reduce the binding strength of metals to the sludge matrix [N2-R2]. The same study also states that microwave treatment can induce immobilization, indicating that it can simultaneously release and then stabilize metals under controlled conditions [N1-F1]. The 1996 EPA comparison study further supports that microwave heating improves reaction control and precision, which can make extraction more uniform and efficient [N4-F2]. Overall, microwave pretreatment appears to make sludge more accessible to reagents by reducing organic barriers, improving porosity, and creating a more reactive environment [N2-R2][N4-F2].

Process conditions that maximize extraction versus those that cause losses are best understood through optimization and comparison studies. The biosolids study reports that microwave treatment can induce immobilization with relatively low exposure time and power, which suggests that lower power and shorter exposure may be sufficient for some applications while avoiding overheating or damage [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The evidence also suggests that sludge composition varies by WWTP, which means that microwave treatment effectiveness can depend on the specific metals and binding forms present [N1-F1].

Microwave stabilization differs from extraction in practical use because stabilization is about making metals less mobile and less likely to leach, whereas extraction is about removing metals from the sludge matrix [N1-R1][N6-R1].
